newsitem.title: CHINA: China's parliament to pass anti-corruption bill.
newsitem.headline: China's parliament to pass anti-corruption bill.

text.p: China's parliament is set to pass an anti-corruption bill that will allow prosecutors to check and freeze banks accounts of graft suspects, the China News Service said on Wednesday.

The draft "Law on Administrative Supervision" would be discussed by the standing committee of the National People's Congress, or parliament, which began a week-long session on Tuesday, the news agency said.

The bill, part of a series of anti-corruption laws expected to be passed by parliament, would let prosecutors investigate a suspect's bank account and ask courts to freeze them when looking into graft, bribery and embezzlement, it said without elaborating.
State media said on Tuesday that China's top prosecutors have vowed to crack down on corruption among the ranks of leading officials in the government and ruling Communist Party.
The call for tougher action to curb growing official graft came as senior leaders considered whether to punish scandal-hit former Beijing Party boss Chen Xitong for dereliction of duty.

In the first 11 months of 1996, Chinese prosecutors had begun action in 77,611 cases of corruption, bribery and economic crime, and had dealt with 33,879 cases, up 9.4 percent year-on-year, the media said.
Corruption was virtually wiped out in the years after the communists took over in 1949 but has staged a comeback after economic reforms were introduced 17 years ago.
